articles.body: Stopping Rogue AI Agents in Real Time: Zero-Disk Ephemeral Sandboxing in 0.12ms Autonomous AI agents (CrewAI, AutoGen, Claude, Cursor) are getting massive privileges: executing terminal commands, querying databases, and making web calls. But with these capabilities comes a growing crisis: rogue agent execution . Whether triggered by indirect prompt injection, zero-width steganography, or context drift, an agent with bash tools can read ~/.ssh/id_rsa , install persistent malware, or exfiltrate environment variables. At Iris Computing (Campfire Creative LLC DBA Iris Computing), we built Iris Sentinel —a zero-disk cryptographic defense gateway and MCP supervisor.

articles.title: How many tokens is 1% of your Claude Code limit?
articles.excerpt: Originally published at limitcast.dev. Anthropic shows how much of your 5-hour and weekly limit you've used, as a percentage. It doesn't say how many tokens that percentage is, and it doesn't say how…
articles.body: Originally published at limitcast.dev . Anthropic shows how much of your 5-hour and weekly limit you've used, as a percentage. It doesn't say how many tokens that percentage is, and it doesn't say how different kinds of tokens count. So I measured it on my own account. 1% of the 5-hour limit was about 166,000 new tokens, or about 11 million cached tokens. A cached token counted roughly 1/67 as much as a new one. That ratio changes what's worth optimizing. Over the two days I measured, new tokens were 2.5% of everything Claude Code sent, and they used about 63% of my limit.

articles.excerpt: The Problem With "Free" Online PDF Converters Executed contracts and legal agreements We set out to build a different model: a document processing suite where files never leave the user device. Here i…
articles.body: The Problem With "Free" Online PDF Converters If you have ever used a standard online PDF compressor, converter, or merger, you have almost certainly uploaded your documents to a third-party server. In many cases, that is an unacceptable risk. Typical PDF payloads contain sensitive data: Executed contracts and legal agreements Patient medical records and diagnoses Banking, tax, and financial statements Proprietary internal company documentation When uploaded, that data travels across external networks, lands on third-party file systems (often indefinitely), and is processed by infrastructure you cannot audit. We set out to build a different model: a document processing suite where files never leave the user device.

articles.title: TrenTorch: learn ML by building your own framework in NumPy (and 350+ browser questions)
articles.excerpt: You can call loss.backward() a thousand times and still not know what it does. TrenTorch fixes that by making you build it. It is two things in one repo: a terminal course of 20 modules where you writ…
articles.body: You can call loss.backward() a thousand times and still not know what it does. TrenTorch fixes that by making you build it. It is two things in one repo: a terminal course of 20 modules where you write your own machine learning framework in raw NumPy, from tensors and autograd up to transformers, and a browser site with 350+ graded coding questions across 12 topic areas. There is no import torch anywhere in the curriculum. No GPU needed. Everything runs on the CPU with NumPy. The CLI needs Python 3.10+, and the web questions run Python 3.12 inside your browser through Pyodide. This guide covers both tracks, plus how to run the question checks if you want to contribute.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.excerpt: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's…
articles.body: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's a still image, video, audio, or text - that "has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence" to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies , as well as restaurants' ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials. Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad … Read the full story at The Verge.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
